draft.title: Box plots and outliers
card: The IQR is \(Q_{3} - Q_{1}\). An outlier is a value below \(Q_{1} - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) or above \(Q_{3} + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\). These two numbers are the fences.
Example: \(Q_{1} = 20\) and \(Q_{3} = 32\). The IQR is 12 and \(1.5 \times 12 = 18\). The fences are \(20 - 18 = 2\) and \(32 + 18 = 50\).
A value exactly on a fence is not an outlier. It must be beyond the fence, so 50 is not an outlier but 51 is.
On a box plot, outliers are drawn as separate points. The whiskers stop at the smallest and largest values that are not outliers.

4.alt: A box plot with the box from \(Q_{1} = 20\) to \(Q_{3} = 32\) and the median at 26. The fences are 2 and 50. The lower whisker stops at 8. The upper whisker stops at 50, which is on the fence, so it is not an outlier. The value 56 is beyond the fence and is drawn as a separate point.

draft.remember: Find the IQR, build the fences with \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), and plot anything beyond them as a point.

a.q: For a data set, \(Q_{1} = 40\) and \(Q_{3} = 52\). Find the upper fence used to test for outliers.
a.why: \(\text{IQR} = 52 - 40 = 12\), and \(1.5 \times 12 = 18\). The upper fence is \(52 + 18 = 70\). Adding only the IQR gives 64, which skips the 1.5.

b.q: A box plot of daily bike hires has \(Q_{1} = 15\) and \(Q_{3} = 27\). Which value is drawn as a separate point?
b.why: \(\text{IQR} = 12\), so the upper fence is \(27 + 18 = 45\). Only 46 is above it. The value 45 is on the fence, so it is not an outlier.
b.clue: A value on the fence is not beyond it.
